cards.front: What is the formal definition, Greek etymology, and primary athletic purpose of plyometric exercise?
cards.back:
Definition: Quick, powerful movements involving a pre-stretch or countermovement that engages the stretch-shortening cycle (SSC) to enable muscle to reach maximal force in the shortest possible time.

Etymology: Derived from the Greek roots plio (meaning 'more') and metric (meaning 'measure').

Purpose: To increase the force and power production of subsequent functional movements by utilizing both the natural elastic components of muscle and tendon and the stretch reflex.

cards.front: According to the mechanical model of plyometrics, what structure serves as the primary 'workhorse' and how does it function?
cards.back:
The Series Elastic Component (SEC) is the mechanical workhorse of plyometric exercise:
  • While it includes some muscular elements, tendons constitute the majority of the SEC.
  • When stretched during an eccentric muscle action, the SEC acts like a spring, lengthening and storing elastic potential energy.
  • If immediately followed by a concentric contraction, this stored energy is released, returning tissues to their unstretched configuration and significantly augmenting total force production.

cards.tag: Mechanical Model: Energy Dissipation and Joint Mechanics
cards.front: Under what conditions will the elastic energy stored within the Series Elastic Component (SEC) fail to contribute to concentric force?
cards.back:
Stored elastic energy dissipates and is lost as heat if:
  • A concentric muscle action does not immediately follow the eccentric stretch.
  • The eccentric phase duration is too long (prolonged amortization).
  • The movement requires too great a range of motion around the given joint (excessive joint displacement).

cards.tag: Neurophysiological Model: Potentiation and Stretch Reflex
cards.front: How does the neurophysiological model explain the increased force production observed during plyometric actions?
cards.back: The neurophysiological model relies on potentiation—an acute change in the force–velocity characteristics of the muscle's contractile components caused by stretch—mediated by the stretch reflex. When an involuntary, rapid stretch occurs, proprioceptors detect the elongation and reflexively increase neural stimulation to the agonist muscle, potentiating force output beyond isolated concentric actions.

cards.tag: Sensory-Motor Circuitry of the Stretch Reflex
cards.front: What sensory receptors and neural pathways mediate the stretch reflex during rapid eccentric loading?
cards.back:
The reflex arc is composed of:
  • Muscle Spindles: Intrafusal proprioceptors sensitive to the rate and magnitude of muscular stretch.
  • Type Ia Afferent Fibers: Sensory nerve fibers that transmit action potentials from stretched muscle spindles to the spinal cord.
  • Alpha Motor Neurons: Efferent neurons synapsing in the ventral root of the spinal cord that immediately transmit excitatory signals back to the agonist extrafusal fibers, producing a reflexive contraction.

cards.front: What is the Stretch-Shortening Cycle (SSC) and what are its three sequential phases?
cards.back:
The Stretch-Shortening Cycle (SSC) is a neuromuscular mechanism that integrates the energy storage capabilities of the SEC with stretch reflex stimulation to maximize muscle recruitment in minimal time. It consists of three sequential phases:
  1. Phase I: Eccentric Phase (preloading and stretch).
  2. Phase II: Amortization Phase (electromechanical delay and transition).
  3. Phase III: Concentric Phase (shortening, elastic recoil, and push-off).

cards.tag: SSC Phase I: The Eccentric Phase
cards.front: What physiological and mechanical events occur during Phase I (Eccentric Phase) of the SSC?
cards.back:
During Phase I (e.g., foot touchdown to the lowest point of descent in a long jump takeoff):
  • Agonist muscle groups are rapidly stretched and preloaded.
  • Elastic energy is absorbed and stored within the Series Elastic Component (SEC).
  • Muscle spindles are stimulated by the stretch and fire sensory action potentials along Type Ia afferent nerve fibers toward the ventral root of the spinal cord.

cards.tag: SSC Phase II: The Amortization Phase
cards.front: Why is the Amortization Phase (Phase II) considered the most crucial phase of the SSC, and what happens at the synaptic level?
cards.back:
The amortization phase is the transitional delay between the end of the eccentric action and the initiation of the concentric action:
  • Synaptic Events: Type Ia afferent nerves synapse with alpha motor neurons in the ventral horn/root of the spinal cord, and alpha motor neurons transmit efferent signals back to the agonist muscle.
  • Crucial Role: Its duration must be kept exceptionally short. If amortization lasts too long, stored elastic energy dissipates as heat, and the stretch reflex fails to potentiate concentric muscle recruitment.

cards.tag: SSC Phase III: The Concentric Phase
cards.front: What dual mechanisms drive force amplification during Phase III (Concentric Phase) of the SSC?
cards.back:
Phase III represents the explosive response to the preceding phases (e.g., gastrocnemius plantarflexion during takeoff) driven by:
  • Mechanical Recoil: Elastic energy previously stored in the SEC is released, adding passive elastic force to the movement.
  • Reflexive Potentiation: Alpha motor neurons discharge onto the agonist muscle, generating a reflexive contraction that recruits additional motor units beyond an isolated concentric action.

cards.tag: Rate of Stretch & Vertical Jump Testing Hierarchy
cards.front: How does the rate of musculotendinous stretch impact performance across the Static Squat Jump, Countermovement Jump, and Approach Jump?
cards.back:
Higher rates of stretch elicit greater spindle activation and elastic storage, establishing a clear vertical jump hierarchy:
  1. Static Squat Jump (Lowest Height): Begins from a static 90° squat with no countermovement; eliminates the eccentric phase, preventing SEC energy storage and stretch reflex potentiation.
  2. Countermovement Jump (Intermediate Height): Utilizes a rapid eccentric dip immediately followed by concentric extension, storing SEC elastic energy and stimulating the stretch reflex.
  3. Approach Jump (Highest Height): Uses a multi-step approach creating an even quicker, more forceful eccentric loading phase; the highest rate of stretch generates maximal neural potentiation and jump height.
